## Overview

The Deori are a Sino-Tibetan ethnic group of Assam and Arunachal Pradesh in Northeast India. Their historical homeland was the greater Sadiya region of the eastern Brahmaputra Valley, including areas around the Dibang, Tengapani and Kundil rivers, while present settlements are distributed across Dhemaji, Lakhimpur, Dibrugarh, Tinsukia, Sivasagar, Jorhat and Sonitpur, as well as adjoining parts of Arunachal Pradesh. The 2011 census recorded 43,750 Deori people, including 32,376 speakers of Deori. The community is divided into Dibongia, Borgoya, Tengaponiya and Pator-goya groups, although the Deori language is principally retained by the Dibongiya. Deori folk culture is especially documented through its creation myth, sacred landscape, priesthood, territorial deities and ritual institutions associated with the Chutia kingdom.

## Material culture

### Architecture

The sources mention the Tamreswari Temple, also called the temple of Dikkaravasini, and the Midiku communal shrine complex of the Dibongiya Deoris. Within the Midiku, the Kundiku is regarded as the abode of Kundi-Mama. The Midiku contains separate ritual spaces for offerings and for the sacrifice of birds and animals, and sacred objects associated with ceremonies are kept there. The sources also record archaeological ruins of a fort with an earthen rampart in the Manabhum region, comparable to sites at Tezu and Hatiduba (Sadiya), together with stone pillars. An inscription dated to 1442 records the construction of a brick enclosure around the temple of Dikkaravasini by Mukta-Dharmanarayana.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

They mention sacred objects kept within the Midiku.

## Music & performance

They do document ritual vocal performance at Tamreswari Temple: the Deoris performed sacrifices, entered the temple and recited ritual hymns. Deori also remains a ritual language. Acharyya and Mahanta found that it continues to be used in prayers and religious rituals by Borgoyan and Tengaponiya communities that ordinarily use Assamese.

Historically, the Deoris served as a priestly section in the Chutia kingdom and officiated in religious rituals associated with its sacred institutions. Four ritual offices were associated with Tamreswari Temple: the Bar Deori (Deori Dema), Saru Deori (Deori Surba), Bar Bharali and Saru Bharali. The Bharalis collected temple dues and provided animals for sacrifice, while the two Deoris performed the sacrifices and recited the ritual hymns.

## Festivals & rituals

They do document a religious system centred on Kundi-Mama, also known as Gira-Girasi or Bura-Buri, regarded as the principal or supreme deity and the creator or supreme power of nature. The Dibongiyas worship Kundi-Mama or Gira-Girasi; the Tengaponiyas are associated with Pisa-Dema, also known as Baliya-Baba or Boliya-Hemata; and the Borgoyans with Pisasi-Dema, identified with Tamreswari or Kecaikhati.

Deori ritual traditions are closely connected with the sacred landscape of Sadiya. Borgoya Deoris were associated with Kecaikhati or Pishasi at Tamreswari Temple, while Dibongiya and Tengapaniya groups maintained the related cults of Gira-Girasi and Pisa-Dema. The Tamreswari ruins and the bolisaal, or sacrificial space, remain important sites of ritual memory and sacred identity.

The Midiku is the traditional communal shrine complex of the Dibongiya Deoris. Its Kundiku is regarded as the abode of Kundi-Mama, and the complex includes ritual spaces for offerings and for the sacrifice of birds and animals. The sources also describe a creation tradition in which Kundi-Mama sent Dudi, the peacock, and Dutimotim, identified as a wagtail, to determine whether land had emerged from the primordial waters. Dutimotim is said to appear on earth around the months of Bhad and Ahin and to return to heaven before the rains begin again.

## Oral tradition & literature

Deori oral tradition includes a creation myth and origin folklore. In the creation myth, the formless supreme deity Kundi-Mama creates the living world after the primordial creator pair sends Dudi, the peacock, and Dutimotim to investigate whether land has appeared from the waters. The tale explains the peacock’s crest and Dutimotim’s ability to move between earth and heaven.

The origin folklore connects the Deoris with the Chutia kingdom. Tamreswari is said to have taken the form of a huge stone that floated in the Dibang River. Four Chutia men, after praying to the goddess, brought the stone to its assigned place, where the king appointed them as priests. They are described as the forefathers of the four Deori clans.

The sources also preserve folklore concerning Jaidham hill, Manabhum and the ancient worship places of the Tengapaniya. The Deori Sahitya Sabha, established in 1965, adopted the Assamese script for Deori publications, including educational materials, prayer books, grammars and dictionaries. Deori remains important for transmitting traditional cultural knowledge.

## Language & religion

Deori belongs to the Sino-Tibetan language family and is generally classified in the Boro-Garo group. Among the four territorial groups, the Dibongiya have retained the language, while the Patorgoyan, Tengaponiya and Borgoyan have shifted largely to Assamese. Deori is spoken in Lohit district of Arunachal Pradesh and in Lakhimpur, Dhemaji, Tinsukia, Sivasagar and Jorhat districts of Assam. The language has been classified as “definitely endangered.” The Deori Sahitya Sabha adopted the Assamese script in 1965.

The traditional religious system is described as animistic and centres on Kundi-Mama, also known as Gira-Girasi or Bura-Buri. Kundi and Mama represent complementary male and female principles. Hindu religious practices have also been adopted through prolonged interaction with Assamese society, while older Deori beliefs and ritual practices remain important. The four principal ritual offices at Tamreswari Temple were the Bar Deori, Saru Deori, Bar Bharali and Saru Bharali.
